newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy leftist coalition party mulls future course.
newsitem.headline: Italy leftist coalition party mulls future course.

text.p: The leader of the Democratic Party of the Left, the largest group in Italy's governing coalition, opened a party congress on Thursday with an appeal for party unity as it mulls its future in Europe.
"We want to create in Italy a left that is more united, tied to Europe," PDS leader Massimo D'Alema told the congress at a sports arena built during the Fascist era.
D'Alema urged the gathering to "re-think and re-launch the cause of the left and see to it that the Italian left becomes more united and stronger".
The PDS, heir to the largest Marxist party in the West, shed communism and changed its name from the Italian Communist Party six years ago, since when it has been trying to woo moderate voters.

D'Alema, who is standing unopposed for re-election when the congress closes on Sunday, wants to transform the PDS still further into a broad social democratic force to consolidate its power in Italian politics.
He said the left was still "too weak and fragile" despite being the pillar of Prime Minister Romano Prodi's nine-month-old government, the first to include former communists in 50 years.
"We are still walking along a path and we have not yet arrived," D'Alema said, warning that some people in the party felt too smug for his liking.

The PDS won just over 21 percent of the vote in last April's general election, propelling the left into power after decades of being excluded from national government for fear of letting communism take hold in Italy.

D'Alema wants the party -- which he took over in 1994 after it suffered an embarrassing loss to former Prime Minister Silvio Berlusconi's centre-right Freedom Alliance -- to appeal to more centrist voters.
His strategy has been to portray the PDS as the trustworthy, serious, option in Italian politics.

Walter Veltroni, the PDS's number two and deputy prime minister, told the congress that before the 1996 elections the opposition centre-right had warned voters Italy faced economic ruin and that foreign investors would flee if the left won.
"The exact opposite happened," Veltroni said to cheers. "We know that even in Italy the left can mean stability."

But Veltroni also said the Italian left had to remain faithful to its ideals. "The left should never put itself in a position where anyone could say that we wanted to change the world but the world changed us," Veltroni said.
One of the hottest debates at the congress will centre on how to change the welfare state and pension system.
The 1,130 delegates will debate a plan to reform social spending, currently one of the thorniest political topics.

Prodi is walking a political tightrope on social spending between the need for financial prudence to meet the conditions for founder membership of a European single currency and the political demands of the hardline Communist Refoundation party.
The centre-left government relies on Communist Refoundation, which was formed from the hard-line wing of the former communist party, for its majority in the Chamber of Deputies (lower house).
